tasks.short: Help sites build a budget and explain where costs should sit.

today.trigger: A site manager, cost-center owner or the controller asks for help on the annual budget, a reforecast, or where a cost should sit (agency labour, warehouse overhead, fleet, a customer start-up).
steps: Pull last year's actuals and the current budget from AFAS Profit by cost center and site (Rotterdam, Tilburg, Venlo).
Rebuild the question in Excel with an allocation key such as hours, shipments, shifts or floor space.
Check wage assumptions against the transport CAO, the warehouse CAO, shift premiums and the three agency rate cards.
Walk through the bridge with the owner and write the recommendation.
File the workbook on SharePoint and mail the conclusion.
drudgery: Re-keying AFAS totals into a fresh workbook for every question.
Searching SharePoint for the allocation key used last year.
Rebuilding the same three-site bridge with small differences in layout.
today.time_sinks: Most hours go to collecting and reshaping numbers. Version chaos in Excel takes the rest. The advice itself is the short part.

lenses.faster: The nightly AFAS extract refreshes the actuals, the budget and the first bridge, so the analyst opens a finished draft. Re-keying totals and hunting for last year's key drop out of the job.
lenses.autonomous: A date on the budget calendar, or a cost question posted in Teams, can start the pack with no diary reminder. The analyst still sends the advice.
lenses.ambitious: At a tenth of the effort the company would keep a cost-to-serve for each large shipper, with flex peaks, shift premiums and the right site inside the rate.
lenses.joy: Nobody will miss rebuilding the workbook. The conversation with the site manager about what the split does to their result is the part worth keeping.
lenses.options: Each request shows the result under hours, shipments, floor space and revenue, with the effect on the site result beside each key.
lenses.altitude: The analyst maintains the allocation rules and the data checks, and spends the hours on splits the rules cannot place.
reach: The controller's first look at whether a cost sits on the right site and in the right entity.
The own-staff, flex and overtime cost bridge that people analytics and payroll rebuild when someone asks a workforce-cost question.

tasks.human_edge: Judging which key a site manager will trust, and when a split would distort a customer's margin or raise a staffing question the works council should hear before anyone treats it as a decision.
tasks.pattern_why: The arithmetic is routine, but the product is advice the business has to trust. The analyst stays the person who stands behind the conclusion, with a draft and several keys ready.

in_practice.trigger: A cost-center owner or the controller asks for a cost split or budget help, or the budget calendar opens a cycle.
steps: Load actuals, the current budget, CAO scale costs and agency rates into a standard bridge from the nightly extract.
Calculate the result under the stored allocation keys and flag missing drivers.
The analyst edits the drivers and writes the conclusion in their own words.
The analyst sends the note and stores the version.
in_practice.human_gate: No allocation advice goes to a site, or into the budget, until the analyst signs the conclusion.
data_needed: General-ledger actuals and budgets by cost center, site and account
Volume drivers: hours, shipments, shifts, floor space
Current transport CAO and warehouse CAO scales and premiums
Agency rate cards for the three staffing firms
The written allocation policy and the chart of accounts
in_practice.logs_to: A SharePoint budget log with one line per request: who asked, which key, the figure advised, the analyst, and the file version.

evidence.claim: Power BI can refresh a cost-center actual-versus-budget bridge from a structured nightly extract.
AFAS Profit already holds the ledger, the cost centers and the budget amounts this bridge uses.
A drafted allocation note still needs a named analyst if a Dutch site manager is going to accept the split. No documented case at a comparable firm is cited.

risks: A wrong key moves profit between Rotterdam, Tilburg and Venlo and the argument arrives in the management meeting.
Person-level pay is unnecessary for this advice and is hard to justify under the AVG. Scales, premiums and cost-center totals are enough.
Advice that reads as a proposal to move work to agencies or to change shifts can become a works-council matter before any decision.
Agency rate cards go stale, and the bridge will look exact while the peak-season invoice does not match.
research_questions: On the last five requests, how many hours went to collecting and reshaping data, and how many went to the conversation and the conclusion?
Are allocation keys written down with an owner, or do they live in last year's workbook?
Will the three site managers accept a fixed set of overhead keys, checked on a sample of large shippers?
Which labour totals can FP&A see with no person-level field in the model?

tasks.short: Read the operating budgets and say which trend changes the need.

today.trigger: During the week, or at the start of a reforecast, the analyst sets the site operating budgets against the latest actuals.
steps: Refresh budget versus actuals from Power BI or export them from AFAS.
Pivot the result in Excel by site, department and cost type.
Look for run-rate shifts in own labour, flex, housing, fleet and the seasonal peak.
Ask operations which movements are one-off and which will persist.
Note the lines that should change in the next budget version.
drudgery: Rebuilding the trend view because the extract and the budget file do not share one grain.
Eyeballing cost centers that only moved with volume.
Copying last month's commentary and changing the figures.
today.time_sinks: Trending three sites and a flex population that swings between about 150 and 300 people takes most of the cycle. Deciding which few movements change the budget is the smaller, useful part.

lenses.faster: The trend view, the volume bridge and a filter for movements that follow volume are ready before the analyst starts. Exporting and re-pivoting drop out.
lenses.autonomous: The nightly AFAS refresh can post the trend pack every Monday, and again when a site's flex hours or revenue cross a band the controller has set.
lenses.ambitious: The company would update budget need by site and by large customer when volume moves, including in the weeks between quarterly reforecasts.
lenses.joy: Scanning flat cost centers is no loss. Arguing which trend is real, with the site manager, is the work people will still want.
lenses.options: Each material trend is shown on a quiet path, the planned peak and a harsh peak, so the budget need is a range with a reason.
lenses.altitude: The analyst sets the bands and the driver definitions, and spends time on trends the rules keep missing.
reach: The controller's early watch on site-margin drift between reforecasts.
A cost-center watch on overtime and absence cost for the people analytics analyst, using totals, not individual sick records.

tasks.human_edge: Telling a one-off shipment, a CAO incidental or a late agency invoice from a new run-rate the budget has to absorb.
tasks.pattern_why: The trend maths can run on the extract, but a change to the budget need is a number the business will hold FP&A to. The analyst releases that change.

in_practice.trigger: The nightly refresh, a Monday schedule, or a cost center crossing its band.
steps: Refresh budget, actuals, volume and flex hours from the AFAS extract.
Compute run-rate, the seasonal pattern and the variance versus the operating budget.
List the lines that would change the budget need, each with its driver and a proposed amount.
The analyst accepts, edits or rejects each proposed change.
Accepted changes wait in the next budget version until the reforecast is approved.
in_practice.human_gate: No operating-budget line changes until the analyst accepts the proposed need.
data_needed: Monthly budget and actuals by cost center and account
Operational volume by site
Flex hours and rates by site and agency
The peak calendar
A list of known one-off items
in_practice.logs_to: A trend log in SharePoint: cost center, driver, proposed change, accept or reject, name and date.

evidence.claim: Scheduled refresh of a finance dataset, with budget-versus-actual measures, is standard Power BI behaviour and matches the nightly extract Noordhaven already runs.
Run-rate and seasonality rules on a cost-center grain can be written and checked without a language model.
Workday Adaptive Planning stores driver-based budget versions and scenarios as a standard product. Noordhaven does not need that product for the first version of this check.

risks: A pack that flags too many lines will be ignored by the third week.
Volume from operations may not match the AFAS month, so the stated driver is wrong.
Treating a seasonal peak as a permanent run-rate inflates the budget and hides the real overspend.
Commentary that names a team or a person drifts into performance monitoring and needs a separate AVG check. Absence cost belongs in the model as a cost-center total.
research_questions: Over the last four reforecasts, what share of budget changes followed a volume move a simple rule would have flagged?
On which day are shipments, hours and shifts available, relative to the AFAS actuals?
In a quiet month, how many lines would the proposed bands flag, and how many of those did anyone act on?
Which accepted budget changes came from something the ledger cannot see, such as a verbal customer promise or a works-council outcome?

tasks.short: Check monthly spend against budget and flag lines that run over.

today.trigger: The month's AFAS actuals are ready, or a department report lands after the close.
steps: Refresh actual versus budget versus forecast by department and site.
Mark lines outside the variance the controller allows.
Add open purchase commitments and agency hours not yet invoiced.
Mail the cost-center owner for an explanation.
Tell the controller which lines should be held or covered by a transfer.
drudgery: Ticking the same underspends every month.
Chasing owners who do not reply before the close meeting.
Stitching agency-portal hours to the ledger so late invoices do not hide an overspend.
today.time_sinks: Chasing explanations and matching the three agencies' hours to AFAS takes longer than spotting the breach. The control is blind until that match is done.

lenses.faster: Breaches, open commitments and uninvoiced flex hours are flagged when the extract and the portal files land. Manual ticking of the department report drops out.
lenses.autonomous: The AFAS period close, or a new agency-hours file, starts the control run with no reminder from the analyst.
lenses.ambitious: The company would see spend in the week it is committed, including flex orders for the peak, while there is still time to hold further orders.
lenses.joy: The monthly tick-and-chase is no loss. Deciding whether a real breach should stop orders, and talking to the owner when the story does not add up, stays.
lenses.options: Each breach shows the forecast effect of holding further orders, of a transfer from contingency, and of accepting the spend in the forecast.
lenses.altitude: The analyst owns the thresholds and the exception list, and stops building the monthly control report by hand.
reach: The bookkeepers' watch on agency hours and goods received that are not yet invoiced, where that hides an overspend.
The controller's first list of variances that could become an audit adjustment.

tasks.human_edge: Deciding whether an overspend is timing, a peak the company chose, or a failure that should stop further orders before the next shift is booked.
tasks.pattern_why: The rule can be written down and the output checks back to the ledger: budget, actual, commitment and open flex orders, against a threshold the controller has signed.

in_practice.trigger: AFAS period close, or a new hours file from a staffing agency.
steps: Load actuals, budgets, open commitments and agency hours onto the same cost center and account.
Flag lines outside the threshold, and lines that uninvoiced flex would push over.
Send the owner a standard question with the figures attached.
The analyst handles flagged lines and any reply that disagrees with the flag.
The controller sees the breaches that are still unexplained at the close meeting.
in_practice.human_gate: A stop on further orders, or a budget transfer, is confirmed by the controller. The flag and the question to the owner go out with the run.
data_needed: Budget, actual and commitment by cost center and account
Agency hours and rates not yet invoiced, by site
The threshold table signed by the controller
The cost-center owner list
The close calendar
in_practice.logs_to: An expenditure-control log: period, cost center, amount over, owner reply, decision, and who released any transfer.

evidence.claim: Budget-versus-actual reporting with a threshold on a scheduled finance extract is standard Power BI use, and Noordhaven already refreshes an AFAS extract nightly.
Comparing budget, actual, commitment and a hours file is a reconciliation with checkable totals. It does not need a language model.
AFAS Profit posts purchase invoices and holds cost-center actuals, which is the ledger side of this control.

risks: A control that ignores uninvoiced flex hours shows a false underspend until the agency invoice arrives.
An automatic block on a warehouse order can stop a shift. The block stays with the controller.
Owners will work around a threshold that is tighter than the seasonality the budget ignored.
Wrong cost-center coding in AFAS creates false breaches and trains people to ignore the list.
research_questions: Of the overspends in the last six months, what share was already visible a week earlier in commitments or agency orders?
How many days typically pass between agency hours worked and the invoice in AFAS?
Are the spend thresholds written down and signed by the controller, or rebuilt in a private sheet each month?
How many control questions a month still have no owner reply at the close meeting?

tasks.short: Check budget files for gaps, bad maths and broken rules.

today.trigger: Cost-center owners send their budget files, almost always Excel, during the planning round.
steps: Check that every required site, cost center and account is present.
Recalculate wage cost from headcount, the relevant CAO scales, premiums and the flex assumption.
Compare the file with the planning instructions and with last year's coding.
Send the holes back to the owner.
Accept the file once it is complete enough to consolidate.
drudgery: Opening many workbooks that do not use the same rows.
Finding a blank that should have been a zero.
Redoing wage maths because someone typed over a formula.
today.time_sinks: Format variation and wage-maths rework take most of the review. The real accuracy questions, volume and flex mix, are a smaller share of the hours.

lenses.faster: Completeness, casting and the rate checks run when the file lands in the SharePoint folder. Manual re-addition and the formula hunt drop out.
lenses.autonomous: A file saved to the submission folder starts the check and returns a defect list to the owner. The analyst does not have to remember who has not submitted.
lenses.ambitious: Every owner would submit once, on one template, and the first file would already meet the rule. The cycle could then be spent on volume and service.
lenses.joy: Policing templates is no loss. Judging an assumption that is complete and still not credible is the part analysts will keep.
lenses.options: The owner sees the file as submitted and the same file restated on the standard CAO and flex assumptions, so the gap has a euro amount.
lenses.altitude: The analyst maintains the checklist, the template and the rate tables, and reviews failed checks and challenged assumptions.
reach: The payroll specialist's check that budgeted wages use the current CAO scales and shift premiums.
The compensation specialist's first look at whether a proposed allowance exists in the warehouse CAO or the transport CAO.

tasks.human_edge: Seeing a file that passes every rule and is still not credible: a flat flex plan through the peak, or a wage budget that ignores a known CAO increase.
tasks.pattern_why: Submissions arrive as uneven workbooks and short mail notes. A language step can place that unstructured file on a standard grid. The arithmetic and the pass or fail stay in ordinary rules. Once every owner uses one locked template, the language step can be dropped.

in_practice.trigger: A budget file is saved to the submission folder or arrives by mail.
steps: Read the workbook and the covering note onto a standard grid: site, cost center, account, amount, driver, assumption.
Run completeness, casting, CAO-scale and flex-rate checks against the source tables.
Produce a defect list the owner can fix, and a short list of assumptions that pass the rules and still look sharp.
The analyst accepts the file into the consolidation or sends it back.
Accepted files lock to a version.
in_practice.human_gate: A submission enters the company budget only after the analyst accepts the check result. A director's override is logged with a name.
data_needed: The submission template and the checklist
The chart of accounts and the valid cost-center list
Current CAO scales and premiums for transport and for warehouse staff
The three agency rate cards
Planning instructions and prior-year actuals
in_practice.logs_to: A submission log: file version, defects, any defect that was waived, who waived it, who accepted the file, and the timestamp.

evidence.claim: Excel can enforce a locked template with required lines and rate formulas before a file is accepted.
Reading a workbook that ignores the template into a reliable grid is plausible, and the parse still needs a check. No documented case at a comparable Dutch firm is cited.
AFAS Profit can supply the valid cost centers and the prior-year actuals the check compares with.

risks: A check that only reads the official sheet will miss numbers parked on a side tab or in a comment.
A waived defect that is not logged is invisible to the auditor and to next year's analyst.
The wrong CAO table, drivers under the transport CAO or warehouse staff under the warehouse CAO, makes every wage budget look conforming.
If the defect note is blunt, owners will send a private file to a director and the check dies.
research_questions: How many budget files arrive per cycle, and how many of them use the official template?
In the last cycle, what share of defects were missing lines, broken formulas or wrong rates, versus an assumption a rule cannot judge?
Which CAO text and which agency rate card is the source of truth, and who updates it?
When a file fails, does the owner fix it, or does a director override the check?

tasks.short: Work out what a plan will cost before it enters the budget.

today.trigger: Operations, HR or a director asks what a plan will cost: a new shipper, an extra shift, a peak flex plan, a site change, or a wave of mandatory certificates.
steps: Pull comparable actuals from AFAS for labour, housing, fleet, supplies and agency spend.
Get the operational case: site, volume, heads, weeks.
Build a cost stack in Excel, including CAO premiums and the agency margin.
Compare the stack with the room left in the site budget and the contingency.
Write the resource figure, the assumptions and the gaps.
drudgery: Building a cost stack from a blank workbook because the last one is private.
Waiting for a volume number that then changes.
Repeating the same premium and flex maths on every request.
today.time_sinks: Finding comparable actuals and restating them for the new case takes longer than the judgment about whether the company should do it.

lenses.faster: Comparable actuals, the rate library and a first cost stack are ready when the request is logged. The blank-workbook hours drop out.
lenses.autonomous: A request that names a site, a volume and a date range can build a draft overnight. A request with a missing driver comes back to the sender the same day.
lenses.ambitious: Every serious operational idea would arrive at the management meeting with a cost and a margin, including the smaller ones that are skipped today because nobody has the hours.
lenses.joy: Rebuilding the stack from scratch is no loss. Pressure-testing the case with the requester, and naming the risk in the rate, is the work worth keeping.
lenses.options: The same plan is costed on a low, base and high case for volume, flex mix and timing, with the budget room shown beside each.
lenses.altitude: The analyst maintains the cost-stack templates and the rate library, and reviews stacks that need a rate the library does not hold.
reach: A first cost, including lost productive hours, for a certificate wave (forklift, VCA, and food safety where a site handles food) that the learning specialist can use.
The accrual shape the accountant needs when a program straddles the month end.

tasks.human_edge: Challenging the operational case: volume counted twice, a flex rate that will not hold when labour is tight, or a saving that is real only after the works council has been consulted.
tasks.pattern_why: The stack pulls several sources and has exceptions, and the resource number will be quoted in a decision. The analyst approves it before it is used.

in_practice.trigger: A named request for the cost of a plan, with a site and a rough volume.
steps: Pull comparable actuals and the rate library: CAO cost, flex, housing, variable supplies.
Build a low, base and high stack and show the budget room left.
List missing drivers and any rate that is outside the library.
The analyst corrects the case and approves one figure.
The approved stack is stored so it can be dropped into the budget version.
in_practice.human_gate: The resource number is not quoted to the board, in a customer conversation, or in the budget until the analyst approves it.
data_needed: Comparable cost-center actuals
A maintained rate library
Remaining budget and contingency by site
The requester's volume, timing and site
Known constraints such as dock capacity and certificate lead times from Studytube
in_practice.logs_to: A program-cost log: request, version, the three cases, the approved figure, the assumptions, and the approver.

evidence.claim: Driver-based cost versions and scenarios are standard in Workday Adaptive Planning. A first version can also live in a controlled table fed by the AFAS extract.
Once the case is structured, building the stack from a ledger extract and a rate table is deterministic and checkable.
The nightly Power BI extract can supply comparable actuals when the grain matches the question.

risks: A stack that looks finished will be quoted to a customer while the volume is still a guess.
Certificate costs and lost hours sit partly in Studytube and with the learning team. Leaving them out understates a new shift.
A plan that cuts own staff or moves work to agencies can be a works-council matter. The cost note must stay a cost note.
Actuals from another site mis-state the case when the mix of work differs between Venlo and Rotterdam.
Candidate data from Recruitee does not belong in the cost stack. Hiring cost, if needed, uses role-level averages.
research_questions: How many plan-cost requests a year get a full stack, and how many hours does one stack take?
For plans approved last year, how far was the stack from the actual cost six months later?
Is there a rate library for CAO cost, flex and housing, and who updates it?
Which drivers can the requester supply in the first message: shifts, shipments, certificates, dock capacity?

tasks.short: Sum up a funds request and recommend a yes or a no.

today.trigger: A manager asks for extra budget (overtime, flex, a repair, equipment, a small project), or the monthly transfer list arrives.
steps: Read the request and the budget still left on that cost center.
Check commitments, year-to-date spend and the forecast.
Write a short summary with a yes, a no, or a yes inside a cap.
Send the recommendation to the controller or the finance director, depending on the mandate.
File the decision so the same euros are not promised again.
drudgery: Restating the remaining-budget arithmetic in every mail.
Chasing a missing amount, period or cost center.
Keeping a private list of approvals so the contingency is not used twice.
today.time_sinks: The summary maths and the search for what is left take longer than the recommendation. The sensitive part is a no, and the explanation to someone senior.

lenses.faster: Remaining budget, commitments and a first recommendation are attached when the request arrives. Rebuilding the 'what is left' table drops out.
lenses.autonomous: A form submission or a request mail starts the summary on its own. The recommendation does not leave until a person releases it.
lenses.ambitious: Small requests inside a pre-agreed envelope would be answered the same day, and the free contingency would stay visible through the peak.
lenses.joy: Rewriting the remaining-budget paragraph is no loss. The hard recommendation, and a no that the manager can understand, stays with the analyst.
lenses.options: The note carries approve, approve inside a cap, defer to the reforecast, or refuse, each with the effect on the site forecast and the contingency.
lenses.altitude: The analyst sets the envelope rules for what can be approved inside the budget and what must go to the finance director, and reviews the refusals and the exceptions.
reach: A short note to the credit and collections officer when the request also worsens cash or days sales outstanding.
The transfer instruction the accountant books after the mandate holder has decided.

tasks.human_edge: A refusal a site manager will accept because the reason is fair, and a yes that does not spend the same contingency twice. Safety, a customer penalty or a CAO entitlement needs a different ear from ordinary overspend.
tasks.pattern_why: The figures and a draft recommendation can be prepared from written rules, but an approval or a refusal carries a name. A person releases it, and the mandate holder confirms it.

in_practice.trigger: A funds request is submitted on a form or by mail.
steps: Read the cost center, amount, period and reason, and send the request back if one of those is missing.
Attach remaining budget, commitments, year-to-date, forecast and the free contingency.
Draft the recommendation from the envelope rules.
The analyst edits the wording and releases the recommendation to the controller or the finance director.
The decision and any AFAS budget transfer are logged before another request can use the same room.
in_practice.human_gate: Nothing is approved, refused or transferred until the analyst releases the recommendation and the person with the mandate confirms it.
data_needed: Remaining budget and commitments by cost center
Open requests not yet booked
The written mandate table
The contingency balance and its earmarks
The request text
in_practice.logs_to: A funds-request log: request, recommendation, decision, mandate holder, and the budget version that was updated.

evidence.claim: Remaining budget, actuals and commitments can be shown from the finance dataset Power BI already refreshes.
AFAS Profit is the place a budget change is stored once someone with the mandate has approved it.
A draft yes or no from written envelope rules is plausible. No documented case at a Dutch logistics company is cited, and the draft should not be sent on its own.

risks: Two requests approved on the same stale remaining budget will overspend the envelope.
A refusal written in a careless tone will be escalated to the director, and managers will stop using the route.
A request tied to safety, a customer penalty or a CAO entitlement is not ordinary discretionary spend. The rule has to recognise it.
A missing log leaves the auditor, and next year's analyst, unable to see why the budget moved.
research_questions: How many funds requests arrive in a month, what is the typical amount, and how long does one summary take?
Is the mandate table written down, including amounts for the controller and for the finance director?
In the last year, how often were two approvals given against the same remaining budget?
How many requests were safety, a customer penalty or a CAO entitlement that a normal envelope rule would have treated as ordinary spend?

tasks.short: Get the regular budget pack and the one-off cuts out.

today.trigger: The close calendar, a management or board meeting, or a director asking for a special cut by customer, site, or own staff versus flex.
steps: Set the contents and the deadline of the pack.
Chase accountants, bookkeepers and site contacts for commentary and late accruals.
Assemble the tables in Excel and place them in PowerPoint or the board note.
Check that the pack ties to AFAS and to the forecast version.
Issue the pack and answer the questions that come back.
drudgery: Chasing the same late commentary every month.
Pasting tables into slides and repairing the formatting.
Rebuilding a one-off cut that a filter on the existing model could have produced.
today.time_sinks: Assembly and chasing people dominate the hours. The judgment is which cut the meeting needs, and whether the tie to the ledger is honest.

lenses.faster: The regular pack is produced from one model on the close calendar, already tested against the ledger. Paste-up into slides drops out for every page that has a standard definition.
lenses.autonomous: The AFAS period becoming ready, or the close-calendar date, starts the regular pack. A special request starts a draft cut. Issue still follows the hold rules.
lenses.ambitious: Every site manager would see the same numbers as the management team on the day the period is ready, and a special cut would be a saved filter.
lenses.joy: Slide paste-up, and chasing a number that is already in AFAS, is no loss. Choosing what the meeting must see, and refusing a cut that does not tie, is the part to keep.
lenses.options: The regular pack can carry the base forecast and two stored scenarios from the same refresh, so a second production run is unnecessary.
lenses.altitude: The analyst owns the report definitions, the tie-out tests and the list of cuts the model must be able to produce, and stops assembling pages.
reach: The first draft of the controller's monthly commentary, written from the same tied pack.
The days-sales-outstanding and cash page the credit officer now builds from a separate extract, using the debtor position and the Rabobank balance already in the close.

tasks.human_edge: Deciding what this meeting must see, and holding back a cut that does not tie to AFAS, including when a senior person wants it the same afternoon.
tasks.pattern_why: A regular pack with a written definition, a structured extract and a tie-out to the trial balance can be produced and checked without a model. Special cuts and broken tie-outs stay with the analyst as exceptions.

in_practice.trigger: The AFAS period is ready for reporting, the close calendar says so, or someone asks for a special cut.
steps: Refresh the standard pack from the nightly extract and run the tie-out tests to the trial balance and the forecast version.
Apply the hold rules, including a site result worse than the amount the finance director has set.
File and send the pack when every test passes and no hold rule trips.
For a special cut, build the draft from the same model and wait.
The analyst repairs breaks, edits commentary and releases anything that failed, tripped a hold, or is special.
in_practice.human_gate: A regular pack that passes the tie-out tests and the hold rules can go out on the calendar. Any break, any special cut, and any page under a hold waits for the analyst.
data_needed: Actuals for the reporting period
The named budget and forecast versions
Tie-out rules to the AFAS trial balance
Hold rules and the distribution list
A written definition of each standard page
in_practice.logs_to: A report-release log: version, tie-out result, hold-rule result, who released it, who received it, and which special cuts were added.

evidence.claim: Power BI already supports scheduled refresh and finance reports on an extract. Noordhaven refreshes AFAS nightly for HR and finance dashboards.
Tying a management pack to a trial balance is ordinary close practice and can be tested with explicit differences.
AFAS Profit is the ledger the pack has to agree with, including the trial balance used for the monthly close.

risks: A pack that ties to a ledger with late or wrong cost-center coding will be trusted and still be wrong.
Sending a surprise site loss to a wide list, before the finance director has spoken to the manager, damages trust in the forecast.
A special cut by person, or a productivity ranking of teams, pulls HR data into a finance report and raises AVG and works-council questions.
Numbers pasted into PowerPoint will fork from the model again if the board pack is maintained by hand.
research_questions: How many analyst hours a month go to the regular pack, and how many to special cuts?
Does the current Power BI model tie to the AFAS trial balance, and what is the usual difference on close day?
Who has to read the pack before a site manager sees a bad result?
Which special cuts were requested more than twice in the last year and should become a standard page?

tasks.short: Tie project and site budgets back to the company pot, including contingency.

today.trigger: Budget consolidation, a new project code, or a question about how much contingency is still free.
steps: List project, customer and site budgets and the company envelope they are meant to sit in.
Check that the parts sum to the parent and that nothing is counted twice.
Identify the contingency and what has already been earmarked for fuel, claims, peak flex or a CAO catch-up.
Investigate lines that do not map, or that map twice.
Report the unallocated remainder and the free contingency.
drudgery: Tracing a project code that was used differently in three files.
Adding the hierarchy by hand.
Explaining a difference that is only a mapping error.
today.time_sinks: Maintaining the map and hunting double counts takes the hours. The judgment is what the contingency is allowed to cover.

lenses.faster: The hierarchy check, and a report that either ties or names the break, runs with the consolidation. Adding the tree by hand drops out.
lenses.autonomous: A new project code, a budget upload or a draw on contingency starts a match run the same night as the AFAS refresh.
lenses.ambitious: Each week the company would see how much contingency is truly free after peaks, claims and wage risk, in time to refuse an ordinary request that is trying to use it.
lenses.joy: Cleaning up mapping errors is no loss. Deciding what may sit in the contingency, with the controller, is the part worth keeping.
lenses.options: The same lines are shown by site, by customer program and by cost type, so a double count is visible in the view where it does damage.
lenses.altitude: The analyst owns the mapping rules and the written definition of contingency, and only sees items that do not match or that someone wants to classify as unforeseen.
reach: The accountant's check that every project code used in the ledger has a parent in the budget.
One view of earmarked contingency for the controller and for the cash forecast.

tasks.human_edge: Judging whether an item is a real contingency case, such as a claim, a fuel spike or a CAO catch-up, or ordinary spend a manager wants outside the operating budget.
tasks.pattern_why: Once the parent map and the contingency categories are written down, the match is a reconciliation. It either ties or it produces a named break. Reclassifying spend into contingency is the exception a person confirms.

in_practice.trigger: A budget upload, a new project or cost center in AFAS, or a draw on contingency.
steps: Apply the stored map from project, customer and site lines to the company envelopes.
Test that children sum to parents and that no line sits in two envelopes.
Show contingency as opening, earmarked, drawn and free, by the allowed categories.
The analyst reviews breaks and any proposed new map.
A map change, or a classification into contingency, is confirmed before that version is used.
in_practice.human_gate: A break or a new mapping is not forced through. Classifying spend as contingency is confirmed by the analyst, and above an amount the controller sets, by the controller.
data_needed: Budget lines at project, site and account level
The parent-child map
The written contingency definition and the current earmarks
Ledger actuals on the same codes
in_practice.logs_to: A mapping and contingency log: the break, the resolution, who changed a map, and who classified an item as contingency.

evidence.claim: Parent-child sums and exception lists are standard Power BI modelling on a budget and actuals table.
AFAS Profit cost centers and project codes can carry this structure when the map is maintained.
Whether Noordhaven's current codes form a clean tree is unknown. The check is only as good as the map.

risks: A clean tie on a bad map hides a double count for the rest of the year.
Parking ordinary overspend in contingency makes the operating budget look healthy and damages trust in the forecast.
Money set aside for a CAO wage increase is not free. Showing it as free means it will be spent.
Project codes opened in the ledger by bookkeepers, and missing from the map, fall out of the envelopes until someone notices.
research_questions: On the last consolidation, by how much did the sum of project and site budgets differ from the company budget?
What was the contingency used for in the last two years, and what share was ordinary operating overspend?
Who can open a cost center or a project in AFAS, and does FP&A see it the same day?
Is there one parent map, and how many budget lines currently have no parent?

role.altitude: The FP&A analyst becomes the owner of the planning system: drivers, allocation rules, control thresholds, tie-outs and the exception list. Sites and the finance director still decide. The analyst designs the checks, reviews what fails, and improves the rules after every close and every reforecast.
reach: Controller: the first flux pass, the pack tie-out, and the list of variances that could become audit adjustments.
Accountant: accrual completeness for agency hours and goods received not invoiced, where it changes the forecast.
Credit and collections officer: the collection assumption inside the cash forecast and the days-sales-outstanding bridge, using the debtor position and the Rabobank balance already in the close.
People analytics analyst and payroll specialist: a cost-center labour bridge for own staff, flex, overtime, premiums and absence cost.
Compensation and benefits specialist: a first scenario on a wage-round or allowance change, priced on scales and headcount, before it enters the budget.
Learning and development specialist: the cost and lost hours of mandatory certificates when a new shift or a peak is planned.
role.ceiling_note: Two analysts cover three sites, and these eight tasks are already about seven tenths of the role. The routine can shrink a long way, but a forecast the business trusts still needs a person in the room when Rotterdam, Tilburg or Venlo disputes the number. The nightly AFAS extract and late agency invoices set the speed. Headcount, shift patterns and the mix of own staff and flex stay with the manager, HR and, where the WOR applies, the works council. The finance director remains the voice to the board. Person-level pay and individual sick records stay out of the planning model under the AVG. Ordinary management forecasting sits outside the EU AI Act's high-risk list, and the design should stay away from scoring individual workers.
skills_to_grow: Write driver definitions, thresholds and tie-out tests that an auditor can re-perform from the log.
Model the Power BI dataset, with enough SQL to control the grain of the AFAS extract.
Read the transport CAO, the warehouse CAO and the three agency rate cards at the level planning needs.
Hold a variance conversation with a site manager and leave with one agreed action.
Keep planning data at cost-center and role level so the AVG question stays simple.
role.ambitious_version: With the checks and the regular packs running, the two analysts would keep a weekly forecast by site and by large customer that operations recognises, with volume, CAO cost, flex mix and free contingency as visible drivers. The month would close on a pack that ties to AFAS when the period is ready, and the analysts would spend their time on breaks, on forecast misses, and on the few decisions the finance director has to take. Days to close and forecast accuracy would show whether this worked.
